q: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead most Cap Classique, and one further grape turns up in it far more often at the Cape than it ever would in Champagne. Which?
exp: It holds high acidity at picking ripeness, which is the first thing a sparkling base needs, and there is a great deal of it in the ground. It appears at both ends of the market, in inexpensive bottles made largely from it and in serious ones where it is blended with the Champagne pair.

q: Westerly air off the Pacific dumps its moisture climbing the Andes and arrives on the far side wrung dry. What does that leave Mendoza?
opts: A humid subtropical climate under constant rot pressure
A desert where no vineyard survives without irrigation
A monsoon pattern of heavy midsummer downpours
A cool maritime climate with reliable summer rain
exp: Rainfall across most of the Mendoza vineyard runs to around two hundred millimetres a year. Sun and drought are the givens; water is the one thing that has to be engineered.

q: Snowmelt reaches the vines along open channels that the Huarpe people began and the Spanish extended. What are those channels called?
exp: The acequia network still governs who draws water and on which day. Rights to it are worth as much in Mendoza as the land they feed.

q: Argentina's first delimited appellation was created in 1989 on the terraces above the Mendoza river and built around Malbec. Which zone earned it?
exp: Lujan de Cuyo took the country's first DOC and San Rafael later became the second. Almost everything else on an Argentine label is registered as a geographical indication instead.

q: Vineyards on stony alluvial fans between roughly nine hundred and fifteen hundred metres make up Mendoza's coolest and most fashionable sub-region. Which is it?
exp: Tupungato, Tunuyan and San Carlos are its three departments. Height buys cold nights, so the wines hold an acidity that the warmer land nearer the city cannot.

q: Chalky, limestone-rich pockets and tense, high-acid Malbec have made one district of Tupungato the most sought-after address in the Uco Valley. Which?
exp: Gualtallary sits high on the Andean side, where free-draining stones lie over calcareous material that is scarce elsewhere in Mendoza. The other three are Lujan de Cuyo districts, lower and warmer.

q: Warm, low-lying land closest to Mendoza city holds many of the province's oldest Malbec and Bonarda vines. Which historic department is it?
exp: Maipu was planted long before anyone thought of farming the high country, and its old vines give a rounder, softer style. The other three are Uco Valley departments.

q: South of the main Mendoza belt, on the Diamante and Atuel rivers, sits the province's second controlled appellation. Which is it?
exp: San Rafael lies lower, warmer and further from the Andes than the Uco Valley. It has a long history in volume production alongside its bottled wine.

q: Whole estates in Mendoza are roofed over with netting stretched above the rows. Which threat does that answer?
exp: A summer hailstorm can strip a vineyard in minutes and it recurs often enough that many growers treat netting as a cost of doing business rather than an option.

q: A hot, dry wind falls off the Andes in late winter and spring, parching flowers and wrecking fruit set. What do Argentines call it?
exp: The Zonda is a foehn wind, warmed and dried by its own descent. The Pampero is its opposite number, a cold southwesterly sweeping up off the plains.

q: Vines at seventeen hundred metres and higher, in a dry valley of red rock in the far north, belong to which province?
exp: Salta farms some of the highest vineyards worked anywhere, with one estate above three thousand metres. Torrontes and a dense, savoury Malbec are its calling cards.

q: Dry, sunny and roughly seventeen hundred metres up, Cafayate lies at the heart of which valley system?
opts: The Alto Valle del Rio Negro
exp: The Calchaqui Valleys thread through Salta, Catamarca and Tucuman. Cafayate is their commercial centre and the source of most Argentine Torrontes with a reputation.

q: Fruit grown above two thousand metres reaches the winery with unusually thick, dark skins. Which condition of altitude explains it?
opts: A far shorter interval between budbreak and harvest
Much heavier rainfall on the upper slopes
Higher average temperatures through the ripening period
The intensity of the ultraviolet radiation
exp: Thinner air filters less ultraviolet light, so the vine answers by thickening the skins, building phenolics and colour as protection. The wide day-to-night swing at the same height is what keeps acidity in place.

q: The Famatina Valley and a long cooperative tradition are the marks of which Argentine province?
exp: La Rioja lends its name to Torrontes Riojano, the best of the three Torrontes. An unusually large share of its crop passes through one very big cooperative.

q: Constant wind, very low humidity and a long cool season along an irrigated river valley describe Argentina's southern vineyards. Which region?
exp: The Alto Valle del Rio Negro was planted with fruit orchards before anyone planted vines. Wind thickens skins and holds disease down, and the latitude gives slow, even ripening.

q: Desert scrub irrigated from a dammed river around San Patricio del Chanar carries Patagonia's newest large plantings. Which province?
exp: Neuquen was built from bare ground in the late 1990s, unlike Rio Negro next door, where some vines are a century old. Malbec and Pinot Noir lead there.
